summary: Discusses the metrics to use when evaluating new or changed congestion control, including transport protocols, TCP changes, application-level control, and active queue management. It notes there is no consensus on a single goal and argues for judging trade-offs among metrics, like throughput, delay, and fairness. It is an informational document from a research group.

plainLanguage.summary: Before you can say a new congestion control scheme is better, you have to say better at what. This memo lists the yardsticks researchers use, from raw speed and delay to fairness between users and how hard the change is to deploy, and points out that they pull against each other.

subtitle: What to measure when you want to know whether a new congestion control scheme is actually better.

tldr.problem: Every new transport protocol, change to TCP or new queue management scheme is judged against something, and there was no shared list of what to measure or how the measures trade off against each other.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists twelve metrics, from throughput and delay through fairness, convergence, robustness and deployability, and notes that most of them can be measured at three levels: the network, the individual flow and the user. It gives the formulas for the common fairness measures and warns that the research community does not agree on what fairness should mean.
tldr.outcome: The document is the first in a series from the Transport Modeling Research Group on how transport protocols are evaluated. It is a survey of the metrics rather than a specification, and it sets no target trade-off.

facts.label: Levels a metric can be measured at

today: RFC 5166 is an Informational document published in March 2008 by the Transport Modeling Research Group, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a survey of the metrics rather than a specification, and it deliberately stops short of choosing targets: the follow-up documents on test scenarios and on methodology are separate.

sections.title: What This Document Is For
sections.content:
The document discusses the metrics to be considered when evaluating a new or modified congestion control mechanism for the Internet. That includes new transport protocols, proposed changes to TCP, application-level congestion control, and Active Queue Management mechanisms in the router. It is the first in a series aimed at improving the models used to evaluate transport protocols.

It does not try to specify every metric a study might consider, and it does not set a target for the trade-offs. Its aim is to show that there is a clear consensus that congestion control mechanisms should be evaluated in terms of trade-offs across a range of metrics rather than by optimizing a single one, even though there is no consensus about which metrics should be optimized or how they should be traded off against each other.

Metrics are considered both for aggregate traffic, taking into account the effect of flows on competing traffic in the network, and for the heterogeneous goals of different applications and transport protocols, such as high throughput for bulk transfer and low delay for interactive voice or video. Different mechanisms may optimize different sets of metrics, with one transport protocol optimized for per-flow throughput and another for robustness over wireless links, and with different degrees of attention to fairness with competing traffic. The goal is a broad view of both the strengths and the weaknesses of a proposed mechanism, so that a reader can see that mechanism X is good at metric A but pays the price with poor performance for metric B.
sections.plainLanguage: You cannot say one congestion control scheme is better until you say better at what. This memo is a shared list of the yardsticks, so that a proposal is judged on all of them rather than on the one its author happened to measure.

sections.title: The Metrics and the Three Levels
sections.content:
The metrics discussed are throughput, delay, packet loss rates, response to sudden changes or transient events, minimizing oscillations in throughput or delay, fairness and convergence times, robustness for challenging environments, robustness to failures and to misbehaving users, deployability, metrics for specific types of transport, and user-based metrics.

Many of these have network-based, flow-based and user-based interpretations. Network-based metrics can consider aggregate bandwidth and aggregate drop rates; flow-based metrics can consider end-to-end transfer times for file transfers, or end-to-end delay and packet drop rates for interactive traffic; and user-based metrics can consider user wait time or user satisfaction with the multimedia experience. The main goal of the document is to explain the set of metrics that can be relevant, not to legislate on the most appropriate methodology for using each general metric. For some metrics, such as fairness, there is no clear agreement in the network community about the desired goals, and the document tries to present the range of approaches.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the yardsticks can be measured at three levels: the network as a whole, the individual connection, and the person using it. A number that looks good at one level can look bad at another, so it is worth saying which level a measurement is at.

sections.title: Throughput, Delay and Packet Loss
sections.content:
Because of the clear trade-offs between throughput, delay and loss rates, it is useful to consider these three together. The trade-off is clearest in terms of queue management at the router: is the queue configured to maximize aggregate throughput, to minimize delay and loss rates, or to compromise between the two? An alternative is a combined metric such as power, defined here as throughput over delay, but the document does not propose a clear target for the trade-off, only that an evaluation should explore the competing metrics. Using flow-based metrics rather than router-based ones, the relationship between per-flow throughput, delay and loss is often given by the transport protocol itself: in TCP the sending rate s in packets per second is 1.2 divided by the round-trip time times the square root of the loss rate p.

Throughput can be measured as aggregate link utilization, as per-connection transfer times, or as user utility functions or wait times. Maximizing throughput is a clear goal of most congestion control mechanisms, subject to application demand and the constraints of the other metrics. The document sometimes distinguishes throughput from goodput, where goodput is the subset of throughput consisting of useful traffic, excluding duplicate packets, packets that will be dropped downstream, and fragments or cells dropped at the receiver because they cannot be reassembled. It does not distinguish between the two in general. In some contexts the aggregate or mean per-flow throughput is enough, in others the distribution of per-flow throughput is needed. Individual applications have their own needs: real-time video traffic can have highly variable bandwidth demands, and voice over IP traffic is sensitive to the bandwidth received immediately after idle periods.

Delay can be measured as queueing delay over time at a router, or as per-packet transfer times, which can include the delay at the sender waiting for the transport protocol to send the packet and, for reliable transfer, the possible delay of retransmitting a lost packet. Users of bulk transfer may care about per-packet times only as far as they affect the per-connection transfer time, while for streaming media per-packet delay can matter a great deal. The average may not capture what users care about: some care about the worst case, or about the tail of the delay distribution. Queueing delay at a router is shared by all flows at a first-in first-out queue, so the queueing delay induced by bulk transfers can matter even when those transfers do not care about per-packet times.

Packet loss rates can be measured at network or flow level. When evaluating the effect of losses or ECN marks on a flow, researchers often use both the loss or mark rate for that connection and the congestion event rate, where a congestion event consists of one or more lost or marked packets in one round-trip time. Some users care about the loss rate only as far as it affects transfer times, and others care about it directly, which is why RFC 3611 defines burst metrics for voice over IP, where a burst is the maximal sequence starting and ending with a lost packet and not including a run of a given number of packets that are not lost. In some cases it is useful to distinguish packets dropped at routers because of congestion from packets lost because of corruption. One network reason to avoid high steady-state loss rates is to avoid congestion collapse in paths with several congested links, where high loss rates mean congested links waste scarce bandwidth on packets that will only be dropped downstream. The retransmit rate can also be high with the goodput correspondingly low even at a low drop rate.
sections.plainLanguage: Speed, delay and loss pull against each other. A router queue can be set to push as much as possible, to keep delay down, or to split the difference. The document also notes that a connection's own formula ties them together, so a change in loss rate changes the sending rate.

sections.title: Response Times and Oscillations
sections.content:
Response times and oscillations are considered together because there are well-known trade-offs between improving response times and minimizing oscillations, and because the scenarios that expose the danger of poor response times are quite different from those that expose the danger of unnecessary oscillation.

One key concern is the response time to sudden congestion, caused by routing or bandwidth changes or by a burst of competing traffic. Mechanisms should respond reasonably promptly to such changes, but should not respond too severely to transient ones, such as a sudden increase in delay that dissipates in less than the connection's round-trip time. Mechanisms also have to contend with sudden changes in the bandwidth-delay product caused by mobility, which are expected to become more frequent and to have greater impact than path changes do today. Because of mobility and the heterogeneity of wireless access types, both bandwidth and round-trip delay can change suddenly, sometimes by several orders of magnitude. This matters most for slowly responding mechanisms such as equation-based congestion control and AIMD, or related mechanisms whose parameters make them slower than TCP.

For an individual connection, one can consider the trade-offs between responsiveness, smoothness and aggressiveness. Smoothness can be defined as the largest reduction in the sending rate in one round-trip time in a deterministic environment with a packet dropped exactly every 1/p packets. Responsiveness is the number of round-trip times of sustained congestion required for the sender to halve its sending rate, and aggressiveness is the maximum increase in the sending rate in one round-trip time, in packets per second, when there is no congestion. Aggressiveness depends on the mode of the transport protocol, and for TCP the aggressiveness of slow start is quite different from that of congestion avoidance.

One goal is stability, in terms of minimizing oscillations of queueing delay or throughput. In practice stability is associated with rate fluctuations or variance, which cause fluctuations in router queue size and therefore queue overflows, which can cause loss synchronization across coexisting flows and periodic under-utilization of link capacity, both general signs of network instability. Measuring the rate variations of flows is therefore a common way to measure the stability of transport protocols, using the coefficient of variation of per-flow transmission rates or the standard deviation of per-flow rates, measured over various time scales. Per-flow rate variations are only one aspect of stability, however: a realistic setting involves multiple flows plus a significant amount of cross traffic with varying rates, so per-flow statistics of a subset of the traffic can mislead, because they measure fluctuations caused in part by adaptation to competing traffic. They are most meaningful when accompanied by statistics measured at the network level, such as the rate variations of aggregate flows observed in bottleneck routers.
sections.plainLanguage: A congestion control scheme has to react quickly when a link really does get busy, and stay calm when the delay spikes for a moment. The measure of calm is how much the sending rate wobbles, and a steady wobble is a sign of an unstable network.

sections.title: Fairness and Convergence
sections.content:
Fairness can be considered between flows of the same protocol and between flows using different protocols, such as TCP-friendliness, and also between sessions, between users, or between other entities. Several measures exist. Jain's fairness index is the square of the sum of the per-connection throughputs divided by the number of users times the sum of the squares of those throughputs; it ranges from 0 to 1, is at its maximum when all users receive the same allocation, and equals k/n when k users equally share the resource and the other n-k receive nothing. The product measure, the product of the individual throughputs, is also used, and in some contexts the product of the powers, called network power. It is particularly sensitive to segregation, being zero if any connection receives no throughput, and for a network with many connections and one shared gateway it is maximized when all connections receive the same throughput. Epsilon-fairness defines an allocation as epsilon-fair when the smallest rate divided by the largest is at least 1 minus epsilon, which measures the worst-case ratio between any two throughput rates.

Other measures account for flows with different resource requirements, such as different utility functions, round-trip times, or numbers of links on the path, and many of them can be described as solutions to utility maximization problems. Max-min fairness requires the smallest throughput rate to be as large as possible, then the next-smallest, and so on, giving absolute priority to the smallest flows; it can be explained by a progressive filling algorithm in which all rates grow at the same pace and each stops growing only when a link on its path reaches capacity. Proportional fairness requires that for any other feasible allocation the sum of the proportional changes is zero or negative, which favours smaller flows but less emphatically than max-min fairness; it can be achieved with logarithmic utility functions. Minimum potential delay fairness, which has been shown to model TCP, minimizes the sum of the inverse of the rates, and is a compromise between the two; it would minimize the average download time if each flow were an equal-sized file. A newer definition of TCP fairness says that a set of TCP-fair flows cause no more congestion than a set of TCP flows would cause, with congestion expressed through queueing delay, queueing delay variation, the congestion event rate and the packet loss rate.

There is no consensus on the fairness goals, and the usefulness of flow-rate fairness has been both challenged and defended. One common argument against fairness between flows with different round-trip times is that long round-trip-time flows consume more resources. Researchers have also noted the difference between the round-trip-time unfairness of standard TCP and the greater unfairness of some proposed changes. A further fairness question is whether a small-packet voice over IP connection, which sends a packet every 10 to 40 milliseconds, should receive the same sending rate in bytes per second as a large-packet TCP connection in the same environment, or the same rate in packets per second.

Convergence times concern the time to reach fairness between an existing flow and a newly starting one, which matters especially for environments with high-bandwidth long-delay flows, and also the time to reach fairness after a sudden change such as a path change, competing cross traffic, or a change in the characteristics of a wireless link. One measure is the delta-fair convergence time: the time for two flows with the same round-trip time to go from shares of 100/101 and 1/101 of the link bandwidth to close to fair sharing with shares of (1+delta)/2 and (1-delta)/2. A similar measure counts round-trip times for two flows to reach epsilon-fairness from a maximally unfair state.
sections.plainLanguage: Fairness means several different things, and the community does not agree on which one matters. Some measures ask whether everyone gets an equal share, others ask whether the slowest flow is protected, and others ask whether the total utility is as high as possible. Convergence measures how long it takes a new connection to reach that fairness.

sections.title: Robustness, Deployability and Method
sections.content:
Congestion control mechanisms are usually evaluated first over environments with static routing in a network of two-way point-to-point links, but some environments bring harder problems, such as corrupted packets, reordering, variable bandwidth and mobility, and new metrics such as energy consumption. Robustness should be explored for paths with reordering, corruption, variable bandwidth, asymmetric routing, router configuration changes and mobility. In general the Internet architecture has valued robustness over efficiency, for instance where there are trade-offs between robustness and the throughput, delay and fairness metrics. In mobile environments the energy consumption of the mobile end node can be a key metric affected by the transport protocol, and for wireless networks the goodput ratio, the useful data delivered as a fraction of all data transmitted, is a useful measure, since a high ratio means efficient use of the radio spectrum and less interference with other users.

Robustness to failures and to misbehaving users is a further goal: receivers that lie to senders about the congestion on the path, or otherwise try to bypass the sender's congestion control, and failures such as routers failing to use explicit feedback or end nodes failing to follow the prescribed protocol.

Deployability is itself a metric, with aspects including the ease of failure diagnosis and the overhead in packet header size or added complexity at end nodes or routers. One key aspect is the range of deployment a new mechanism needs: only at the sender, as with NewReno in TCP; only at the receiver, as with delayed acknowledgements; at both ends, as with SACK TCP; at a single router, as with Random Early Detection; at all routers along the path; or at both end nodes and all routers along the path, as with XCP. Some mechanisms also have deployment issues with IPsec, IP in IP, MPLS, other tunnels, or with non-router queues such as those in Ethernet switches. Another issue is the complexity of the code: is floating point math required, how much new state must be kept, and who holds that state. The document does not suggest reducing deployability to a single number, but lists these as issues to consider.

Some transports need modified metrics, for quality-of-service enabled environments or for below-best-effort traffic. An alternative approach is to evaluate in terms of user metrics such as user satisfaction or application-specific utility functions, which would require defining a range of user metrics or utility functions for the applications under consideration. The document relates its metrics to those of the IP Performance Metrics Working Group, which gives concrete, well-defined metrics with a measurement methodology for connectivity, delay and loss, delay variation, loss patterns, reordering, bulk transfer capacity and link capacity; the difference is that the IPPM metrics are for operators, end users and testing groups, while these are for analysis, simulation and experiment. On methodology, the document notes it is important to evaluate over a wide range of environments, link bandwidths, congestion levels and degrees of statistical multiplexing, over a range of scenarios including typical connection sizes and round-trip times, and to compare a new mechanism with the current TCP standards.
sections.plainLanguage: A scheme also has to be practical. How many routers and end points have to change? How much extra state does it need? Can you work out what went wrong when it fails? And how the packets should be measured depends on where in the network you look.
